*If there is reproach, then welcome and hail, and reproach is due to her with us, and she has been wronged.*

﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾: that is, it is spread out and its mountains are leveled. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It will be stretched like a hide (*tuddu madda al-adīm*)," because when a hide (*adīm*) is stretched, every fold in it disappears, and it becomes extended and level. Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd said: its extent will be increased by such-and-such, so that the creatures may stand upon it for the reckoning, until none of the human beings has anything but the place of his foot, because of the multitude of creatures upon it. It has already been mentioned in Sūrat Ibrāhīm [[See vol. 9, p. 383.]] that the earth will be replaced by another earth, which is *al-sāhirah* according to Ibn ʿAbbās, as was previously reported from him [[See p. 196 of this part.]].

﴿And casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾: that is, it brings out its dead and empties itself of them. Ibn Jubayr said: it casts out what is in its belly of the dead, and empties itself of those upon its back of the living. It was also said: it casts out what is in its belly of its treasures and minerals, and empties itself of them, meaning its inside is emptied so that nothing is left in its belly. This indicates the magnitude of the matter, just as a pregnant woman casts out what is in her belly in severe distress. It was also said: it empties itself of what is upon its back of its mountains and seas. It was also said: it casts out what it has been entrusted with, and empties itself of what it has been made to keep, because Allah entrusted it to His servants, living and dead, and made it keep His lands for cultivation and sustenance.

﴿And hearkens to its Lord, as it must﴾: that is, in casting out its dead. ﴿As it must﴾: that is, it is fitting for it to listen to His command. Concerning the answer to *idhā* (when), there is disagreement. Al-Farrāʾ said: the answer is *adhinat*, and the *wāw* is superfluous, and likewise *wa-alqat*. Ibn al-Anbārī said: some exegetes said the answer of *idhā al-samāʾu inshaqqat* is *adhinat*, and claimed the *wāw* is inserted. This is an error, because the Arabs do not insert the *wāw* except with *ḥattā idhā* as in His saying, ﴿until, when they reach it, its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 71], and with *lammā* as in His saying, ﴿So when they had both submitted and he had thrown him down upon his forehead, and We called to him﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 103–104], meaning "We called to him." It was also said: the answer is a hidden *fāʾ*, as if He said: "When the sky splits asunder, then, O human being, indeed you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet it." It was also said: its answer is what is indicated by ﴿and you will meet it﴾, meaning: when the sky splits asunder, the human being will meet his toil. It was also said: there is inversion, meaning: "O human being, indeed you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet it when the sky splits asunder." This was said by al-Mubarrad. It was also said: some of them had asked about the time of the Hour, so they were told: when its signs appear, the Hour will come, and then you will see the consequence of your denial of it. The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 84, verses 6–9:

Allah's words: ﴿O you who have been given the Book, you are toiling towards your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him.﴾ By "al-insan" (the human being) is meant the species, that is, O son of Adam. Likewise, Sa'id narrated from Qatadah: "O son of Adam, your toil is indeed feeble, so whoever is able to make his toil be in obedience to Allah, let him do so, and there is no power except with Allah." It has also been said that it refers to a specific person. Muqatil said: it means al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad. It is also said: it means Ubayy ibn Khalaf. And it is said: it means all the disbelievers, meaning, "O disbeliever, you are toiling."

In the speech of the Arabs, "al-kadh" means labour and earning. Ibn Muqbil said:

"Time is only two periods: in one of them I die, and in the other I strive, seeking a living."

Another said:

"The cheerfulness of every good life has passed away, and I remain toiling and exhausted for life."

That is, "I work." Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas: ﴿you are toiling﴾ means "you are returning," ﴿towards your Lord with toil﴾ means "a return that cannot be avoided." ﴿And you will meet Him﴾ means "meeting your Lord." It has also been said: "meeting your deeds." Al-Qutabi said: ﴿you are toiling﴾ means "you are a worker, exerting yourself in your livelihood, toward meeting your Lord." The "mulaqah" (encounter) has the meaning of "liqa'" (meeting): that you meet your Lord with your deeds. It has also been said: it means you encounter the record of your deeds, because the work has ended; for this reason He said: ﴿So as for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾.

Allah's words: ﴿So as for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning﴾, and he is the believer, ﴿with no scrutiny in it.﴾ This has been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) through the hadith of Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is called to account on the Day of Resurrection will be punished." She said: I said, "O Messenger of Allah, has not Allah said: ﴿So as for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning﴾?" He said: "That is not the reckoning; that is merely the presentation. Whoever has his reckoning scrutinised on the Day of Resurrection will be punished." It was recorded by al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi, and he said: it is a hasan sahih hadith.

﴿And he will return to his family, joyful﴾: his wives in Paradise, from the al-Hur al-'Ayn (the wide-eyed, lovely companions of Paradise), ﴿joyful﴾, meaning delighted and content. It is said that it was revealed concerning Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad, who was the first to emigrate from Makkah to Madinah. It has also been said: "to his family who were with him in the world," so that he may inform them of his deliverance and safety. The first view is the statement of Qatadah, meaning: to his family whom Allah has prepared for him in Paradise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 84, verse 10–15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But as for him who is given his record behind his back﴾. It was revealed concerning al-Aswad ibn Abd al-Asad, the brother of Abu Salamah, as said by Ibn Abbas. Then it is general in application to every believer and disbeliever. Ibn Abbas said: He extends his right hand to take his record, and an angel pulls it, so it dislocates his right hand, and he takes his record with his left from behind his back. Qatadah and Muqatil said: The bones of his chest and his ribs are unlocked, then his hand is inserted and brought out from his back, and so he takes his record in that manner.

(﴿Then he will call for destruction﴾) i.e., for annihilation, so he will say: "Woe to me! Woe to my destruction!"

(﴿And he will burn in the Blaze﴾) i.e., he will enter the Fire until he is roasted by its heat. Al-Haramayn, Ibn Amir and al-Kisa'i recited (وَيُصْلَى, wayuṣlā) with a dammah on the yaa, a fathah on the saad and a shaddah on the laam, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then into Hellfire, burn him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 31] and His saying: ﴿and the burning of Hellfire﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 94]. The rest recited (وَيَصْلَى, wayaṣlā) with a fathah on the yaa and without a shaddah, an intransitive verb, due to His saying: ﴿except him who is to burn in Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 163], His saying: ﴿who will enter the greatest Fire﴾ [al-A'la: 12], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, they will surely burn in Hellfire﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 16]. A third reading, transmitted by Aban from Asim, Kharijah from Nafi', and Isma'il al-Makki from Ibn Kathir, is (وَيُصْلَى, wayuṣlā) with a dammah on the yaa, a sukun on the saad and a fathah on the laam, unshaddaded, as it is read (وَسَيُصْلَوْنَ, wasayuṣlawna) with a dammah on the yaa. Likewise in "al-Ghashiyah," it has also been read: (تَصْلَى نَارًا, taṣlā nāran). Both are dialects: ṣalā and aṣlā, like His saying: "nazala" and "anzala."

(﴿Indeed, he had been among his people⦋in the world⦌ joyful﴾). Ibn Zayd said: Allah described the people of Paradise in the world with fear, sorrow, weeping and compassion, so He recompensed them with bliss and joy in the Hereafter, and he recited the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we were before this among our people in fear. But Allah has been gracious to us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind﴾ [al-Tur: 26–27]. He said: And He described the people of the Fire as being joyful in the world, laughing in it and jesting. So He said: ﴿Indeed, he had been among his people joyful﴾.

(﴿Indeed, he thought he would never return﴾) i.e., he would never return alive, resurrected, to be reckoned, and then rewarded or punished. It is said: ḥāra yaḥūru, when he returned. Labid said:

"And a man is but like a meteor, its light
returns to ashes after it had been blazing."

Ikrimah and Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: yaḥūru is a word in Abyssinian (Ethiopic), and its meaning is "returns." It is possible that the two words coincide, as they are a word of derivation, and from it comes "al-khubz al-ḥuwwārā" (the fine white bread), because it returns to whiteness. Ibn Abbas said: I did not know what yaḥūr meant until I heard a Bedouin woman calling her little daughter: "Ḥūrī," i.e., return to me. So al-ḥawr in the speech of the Arabs means return, and from it is his peace be upon him saying: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from ḥawr after kawr," meaning: from returning to deficiency after increase. Likewise al-ḥūr with a dammah. In the proverb: "Ḥūrun fī maḥāratin" (a loss within a loss), i.e., deficiency upon deficiency. It is said of a man when his affair is turning backward. The poet said:

"They hurried past the easy chewing and gulped down, and blame remains, while the people's provision is in ḥūr."

Al-ḥūr also means: the noun from your saying: "The grinder ground and did not return (aḥārat) anything," i.e., it did not return any of the flour. Al-ḥūr also means destruction. The rajiz said: [the poet is al-Ajjaj]:

"In a well of ḥūr, neither traveling nor poetry" (lā being extra). Abu Ubaydah said: i.e., a well of ḥūr, and "lā" is superfluous. It is also narrated as "ba'd al-kawn" [the kawn here: the verbal noun of the complete kāna, saying kāna yakūnu kawnan: i.e., existed and settled. (al-Nihayah)], and its meaning is from the dispersal of a matter after its completion. Ma'mar was asked about "ḥawr after kawn," and he said: It is al-kuntiyy. Abd al-Razzaq said to him: And what is al-kuntiyy? He said: A man who is righteous and then turns into an evil man. Abu Amr said: It is said of a man when he grows old: kuntiyy, as if he were ascribed to his saying: "I was in my youth such-and-such." He said:

"So I have become a kuntiyy and have become one who walks with difficulty, and the worst of a man's traits is 'I was' and 'I am walking with difficulty.'"

Ajana al-rajul: when he rises leaning on the ground from old age. Ibn al-A'rabi said: The kuntiyy is the one who says: "I was young, I was brave," and the kani is the one who says: "I had wealth and I used to give gifts; I had horses and I used to ride."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yes﴾, i.e., the matter is not as he thought; rather he will return to Us and come back.

(﴿Indeed, his Lord was ever Seeing of him﴾) before He created him, knowing that his return is to Him. It was also said: "Yes, he will surely return and surely come back." Then He resumed, saying: Indeed, his Lord was ever Seeing of him from the day He created him until He resurrected him. It was also said: knowing what had preceded for him of wretchedness and happiness.

(﴿Indeed, his Lord was ever Seeing of him﴾) before He created him, knowing that his return is to Him. It was also said: "Yes, he will surely return and surely come back." Then He resumed, saying: Indeed, his Lord was ever Seeing of him from the day He created him until He resurrected him. It was also said: knowing what had preceded for him of wretchedness and happiness.

And the word shafaq is applied to red ochre (al-maghra).

*"A king, nobler than kings, whose hands pour out for those who ask, not sparing."*

God's words, "And the night and what it drives together" (wa-l-layli wa-ma wasaq): that is, it gathers, unites and wraps up. Its origin is from the sultan's force and anger. Had He not come out to the servants through the door of mercy, the servants could not have endured His coming. But He came out through the door of mercy, so He was gentle with them, and the creatures became calm in Him, then they were startled, gathered together and withdrew, and each returned to its shelter, and it settled there from its terror. This is His words, "And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein" (Qur'an 28:73), that is, by night, "and that you may seek of His bounty" (28:73), that is, by day, as previously mentioned. He means that there is nothing of that in his hand, just as there is nothing in the hand of one who grasps water. When the night covers the mountains, trees, seas and earth, and they are gathered under it, then it has "wasaqa" them. Al-wasq is joining one thing to another. You say: "Wasaqtuhu, asiquhu, wasqan." (This is the words of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, whose first verse is: "I lied against you; you do not cease to track me.")

Ibn Jubayr said: "'And what it wasaq' means what is done in it, meaning the night prayer (tahajjud) and seeking forgiveness at dawn." The poet said:

That is, like one who acts.

God's words, "And the moon when it becomes full" (wa-l-qamari idha-t-satqa): that is, completed, gathered and became whole. Al-Hasan said: "Ittasaqa: it became full and gathered." *"You will surely ride stage after stage"* (la-tarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq). Al-Sha'bi said: "You will surely ride, O Muhammad, heaven after heaven, and degree after degree, and rank after rank, in nearness to God Most High." Ibn Mas'ud said: "You will surely ride the heaven state after state, meaning its states which God described: splitting, folding up, sometimes being like molten metal and sometimes like oil." From Ibrahim, from 'Abd al-A'la: "Tabaqan 'an tabaq," he said: "The heaven is turned state after state. It becomes red like oil (al-dihan), and it becomes like molten metal (al-muhl)." It was also said: "You will surely ride, O human being, state after state: from being a drop of sperm, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then living and dead, and rich and poor." So the address is to the human being mentioned in His words: *"O man, you are labouring toward your Lord"* (84:6), which is a generic name, meaning people.

The rest read *la-tarkabunna* with a damma on the ba', as address to people. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this, and said: "Because the meaning is more fitting to people than to the Prophet ﷺ, given what was mentioned before this verse: *'As for him who is given his record in his right hand... and as for him who is given his record behind his back'* (84:7–10)." That is: you will surely ride state after state of the horrors of the Resurrection, or you will surely follow the practice of those before you in denying and fabricating against the prophets.

I say: all of this is intended, and hadiths have come with that. Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali, from Jabir, may God be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Indeed, the son of Adam is in heedlessness of what God Mighty and Majestic created him for. Indeed, God, there is no god but He, when He wills to create him, says to the angel: 'Write his provision, his traces, his term, and write whether he will be wretched or happy.' Then that angel ascends, and God sends another angel who guards him until he reaches maturity. Then God sends two angels who write his good deeds and his evil deeds. When death comes to him, those two angels ascend. Then the angel of death, peace be upon him, comes to him and takes his soul. When he is placed in his grave, the soul is returned to his body. Then the angel of death ascends. Then the two angels of the grave come to him and test him, then they ascend. When the Hour is established, the angel of good deeds and the angel of evil deeds descend upon him, and they bring forth a book tied to his neck, then they both attend him, one driving and the other as witness." Then God Mighty and Majestic says: *"You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp"* (Qur'an 50:22). The Messenger of God ﷺ said regarding *"You will surely ride stage after stage"*: "State after state." Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, before you is a great matter, so seek help in God the Mighty."

This hadith includes the states that befall the human being from the time he is created until the time he is resurrected, and all of them are hardship after hardship: life, then death, then resurrection, then recompense, and in each of these states there are hardships.

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "You will surely follow [in the narration of al-Bukhari: 'You will surely follow'] the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, so that if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it." They said: "O Messenger of God, the Jews and the Christians?" He said: "Who else?" Al-Bukhari recorded it.

As for the statements of the commentators: 'Ikrimah said: "State after state: weaned after suckling, and an old man after youth." The poet said:

*"Thus is the man: if a term is granted to him, after it he will ride stage after stage."*

And from Makhul: "Every twenty years you will find a matter you were not upon." Al-Hasan said: "A matter after a matter: ease after hardship, and hardship after ease; wealth after poverty, and poverty after wealth; health after sickness, and sickness after health." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "A station after a station: some people were humble in this world and are raised up in the Hereafter, and some people were exalted in this world and are brought low in the Hereafter." It has also been said: "A station from a station, and a tabaq (stratum, layer) from a tabaq." That is because whoever is upon righteousness is drawn by it to a righteousness above him, and whoever is upon corruption is drawn by it to a corruption above him, for everything moves toward its like. Ibn Zayd said: "You will surely pass from the stratum of this world to the stratum of the Hereafter."

Ibn Abbas said: "The hardships and terrors are: death, then resurrection, then the reckoning (al-'ard)." The Arabs say of one who has fallen into a severe matter: "He has fallen into the daughters of tabaq," and "one of the daughters of tabaq." From this it was said of a severe calamity: "Umm tabaq" (mother of tabaq), and "one of the daughters of tabaq." Its origin is from the snakes, since a snake is called "Umm tabaq" because it coils (tahwiha) around things.

In the language, tabaq means a state, as we have described. Al-Aqra' ibn Habis al-Tamimi said:

"I am a man who has milked the age to its last sips,
and a tabaq from it has driven me from one tabaq to another."

This is the clearest proof of the createdness of the world and of the existence of the Maker. The wise have said: "Whoever is in one state today and in another state tomorrow should know that his governance belongs to other than himself." It was said to Abu Bakr al-Warraq: "What is the proof that this world has a Maker?" He said: "The transformation of conditions, the weakness of strength, the frailty of the pillars, the subjugation of intention, and the abrogation of resolve."

It is also said: "A tabaq of people came to us, and a tabaq of locusts," meaning a group. And al-Abbas's words in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"He is transferred from loin to womb;
when one age passes, another tabaq appears."

That is, a generation of people. Tibaq al-ard means its filling (i.e., covering the earth). Tabaq also means a thin bone that separates two vertebrae. It is said: "A tabaq of the night has passed, and a tabaq of the day," meaning most of it. Tabaq is the singular of atbaq, so it is a homonym (mushtarak).

It is read as "latarkabunna" with a kasra on the ba', addressing the self (nafs), and as "layarkabanna" with a ya', meaning "the human being will surely ride." "'An tabaq" is in the position of an accusative as an attribute of "tabaqan," meaning a tabaq that exceeds another tabaq; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "latarkabunna," meaning you will surely ride tabaqs exceeding one another, or exceeding, or being exceeded, according to the reading.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ That is: what prevents them from believing after the signs have become clear to them and the proofs have been established? This is a rhetorical question of denunciation. It has also been said that it is an expression of wonder, meaning: be amazed at them for abandoning faith despite these signs.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾, that is, they do not pray. In the Sahih it is reported that Abu Hurayrah recited "Idhā al-samā' inshaqqat" and prostrated in it, and when he finished he informed them that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had prostrated in it. Malik said: it is not one of the obligatory prostrations ('azā'im al-sujud, the prostrations of recitation that are required), because the meaning is "they do not submit and do not obey in acting upon its obligations." Ibn al-Arabi said: "The correct view is that it is one of them, and this is the narration of the people of Madina from him, and the Qur'an and the Sunnah support it." Ibn al-Arabi said: "When I led the people in prayer, I left off reciting it, because if I prostrated they would denounce it, and if I left it out it would be a shortcoming on my part. So I avoided it, except when I pray alone." This is the realization of the promise of the Truthful (ﷺ) that the known will become unknown and the unknown will become known. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'A'isha: "Were it not for the recent nearness of your people to disbelief, I would have demolished the House and restored it upon the foundations of Ibrahim."

Our shaykh Abu Bakr al-Fihri used to raise his hands at the bowing (ruku') and when rising from it, and this is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i, and the Shi'a also do it. One day he came to me at the guard post of Ibn al-Shawwa' in al-Thaghr, the place where I taught, at the time of the Dhuhr prayer. He entered the mosque from that guard post and went forward to the row while I was sitting at the rear of it, on the openings of the sea, seeking the breeze because of the intense heat. In the same row with me was Abu Thimna, the captain and commander of the sea, with some of his companions, waiting for the prayer and looking out at the ships beneath the harbour. When the shaykh raised his hands in bowing and in rising from it, Abu Thimna and his companions said: "Do you not see this easterner, how he entered our mosque? Get up and kill him and throw him into the sea, so that no one sees you." My heart flew from between my ribs, and I said: "Glory be to Allah, this is al-Turtushi, the jurist of the age!" They said to me: "Why does he raise his hands?" I said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to do so, and this is the position of Malik, in the narration of the people of Madina from him." I kept calming them and silencing them until he finished his prayer. I then went with him to the lodging in the guard post, and he saw the change in my face, and he disapproved of it and asked me, and I informed him. He laughed and said: "And from where for me to be killed over a sunnah?" I said to him: "This is not permissible for you, for you are among a people who, if you stand up to it, will rise against you, and perhaps your blood will be shed." He said: "Leave this talk, and turn to something else."

God's words, "And the moon when it becomes full" (wa-l-qamari idha-t-satqa): that is, completed, gathered and became whole. Al-Hasan said: "Ittasaqa: it became full and gathered." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It became even (istawa)." Qatadah said: "It became round." Al-Farra' said: "Its ittisaq is its becoming full and even on the nights of the full moon. It is an iftia'l from al-wasq, which is gathering. It is said: 'I wasaqtuhu, fa-ttasaqa,' as one says: 'I wasaltuhu, fa-ttasala.' It is also said: 'The affair of so-and-so is musttasiq,' meaning gathered upon righteousness and well-ordered. It is said: 'Ittasaqa al-shay',' when it followed in succession."

*"You will surely ride stage after stage"* (la-tarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq). Abu 'Amr, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, Masruq, Abu Wa'il, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *la-tarkabanna* with a fatha on the ba', addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "You will surely ride, O Muhammad, state after state," as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Sha'bi said: "You will surely ride, O Muhammad, heaven after heaven, and degree after degree, and rank after rank, in nearness to God Most High." Ibn Mas'ud said: "You will surely ride the heaven state after state, meaning its states which God described: splitting, folding up, sometimes being like molten metal and sometimes like oil." From Ibrahim, from 'Abd al-A'la: "Tabaqan 'an tabaq," he said: "The heaven is turned state after state. It becomes red like oil (al-dihan), and it becomes like molten metal (al-muhl)." It was also said: "You will surely ride, O human being, state after state: from being a drop of sperm, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then living and dead, and rich and poor." So the address is to the human being mentioned in His words: *"O man, you are labouring toward your Lord"* (84:6), which is a generic name, meaning people.

The rest read *la-tarkabunna* with a damma on the ba', as address to people. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this, and said: "Because the meaning is more fitting to people than to the Prophet ﷺ, given what was mentioned before this verse: *'As for him who is given his record in his right hand... and as for him who is given his record behind his back'* (84:7–10)." That is: you will surely ride state after state of the horrors of the Resurrection, or you will surely follow the practice of those before you in denying and fabricating against the prophets.

I say: all of this is intended, and hadiths have come with that. Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali, from Jabir, may God be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Indeed, the son of Adam is in heedlessness of what God Mighty and Majestic created him for. Indeed, God, there is no god but He, when He wills to create him, says to the angel: 'Write his provision, his traces, his term, and write whether he will be wretched or happy.' Then that angel ascends, and God sends another angel who guards him until he reaches maturity. Then God sends two angels who write his good deeds and his evil deeds. When death comes to him, those two angels ascend. Then the angel of death, peace be upon him, comes to him and takes his soul. When he is placed in his grave, the soul is returned to his body. Then the angel of death ascends. Then the two angels of the grave come to him and test him, then they ascend. When the Hour is established, the angel of good deeds and the angel of evil deeds descend upon him, and they bring forth a book tied to his neck, then they both attend him, one driving and the other as witness." Then God Mighty and Majestic says: *"You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp"* (Qur'an 50:22). The Messenger of God ﷺ said regarding *"You will surely ride stage after stage"*: "State after state." Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, before you is a great matter, so seek help in God the Mighty."

This hadith includes the states that befall the human being from the time he is created until the time he is resurrected, and all of them are hardship after hardship: life, then death, then resurrection, then recompense, and in each of these states there are hardships.

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "You will surely follow [in the narration of al-Bukhari: 'You will surely follow'] the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, so that if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it." They said: "O Messenger of God, the Jews and the Christians?" He said: "Who else?" Al-Bukhari recorded it.

As for the statements of the commentators: 'Ikrimah said: "State after state: weaned after suckling, and an old man after youth." The poet said:

*"Thus is the man: if a term is granted to him, after it he will ride stage after stage."*

And from Makhul: "Every twenty years you will find a matter you were not upon." Al-Hasan said: "A matter after a matter: ease after hardship, and hardship after ease; wealth after poverty, and poverty after wealth; health after sickness, and sickness after health." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "A station after a station: some people were humble in this world and are raised up in the Hereafter, and some people were exalted in this world and are brought low in the Hereafter." It has also been said: "A station from a station, and a tabaq (stratum, layer) from a tabaq." That is because whoever is upon righteousness is drawn by it to a righteousness above him, and whoever is upon corruption is drawn by it to a corruption above him, for everything moves toward its like. Ibn Zayd said: "You will surely pass from the stratum of this world to the stratum of the Hereafter."

Ibn Abbas said: "The hardships and terrors are: death, then resurrection, then the reckoning (al-'ard)." The Arabs say of one who has fallen into a severe matter: "He has fallen into the daughters of tabaq," and "one of the daughters of tabaq." From this it was said of a severe calamity: "Umm tabaq" (mother of tabaq), and "one of the daughters of tabaq." "I am a man who has milked the age to its last sips,
and a tabaq from it has driven me from one tabaq to another."

This is the clearest proof of the createdness of the world and of the existence of the Maker. The wise have said: "Whoever is in one state today and in another state tomorrow should know that his governance belongs to other than himself." It was said to Abu Bakr al-Warraq: "What is the proof that this world has a Maker?" He said: "The transformation of conditions, the weakness of strength, the frailty of the pillars, the subjugation of intention, and the abrogation of resolve."

"He is transferred from loin to womb;
when one age passes, another tabaq appears."

That is, a generation of people. Tibaq al-ard means its filling (i.e., covering the earth). Tabaq also means a thin bone that separates two vertebrae. Ibn al-Arabi said: "The correct view is that it is one of them, and this is the narration of the people of Madina from him, and the Qur'an and the Sunnah support it." Ibn al-Arabi said: "When I led the people in prayer, I left off reciting it, because if I prostrated they would denounce it, and if I left it out it would be a shortcoming on my part. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'A'isha: "Were it not for the recent nearness of your people to disbelief, I would have demolished the House and restored it upon the foundations of Ibrahim."

Our shaykh Abu Bakr al-Fihri used to raise his hands at the bowing (ruku') and when rising from it, and this is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i, and the Shi'a also do it. One day he came to me at the guard post of Ibn al-Shawwa' in al-Thaghr, the place where I taught, at the time of the Dhuhr prayer. He entered the mosque from that guard post and went forward to the row while I was sitting at the rear of it, on the openings of the sea, seeking the breeze because of the intense heat. In the same row with me was Abu Thimna, the captain and commander of the sea, with some of his companions, waiting for the prayer and looking out at the ships beneath the harbour. When the shaykh raised his hands in bowing and in rising from it, Abu Thimna and his companions said: "Do you not see this easterner, how he entered our mosque? Get up and kill him and throw him into the sea, so that no one sees you." My heart flew from between my ribs, and I said: "Glory be to Allah, this is al-Turtushi, the jurist of the age!" They said to me: "Why does he raise his hands?" I said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to do so, and this is the position of Malik, in the narration of the people of Madina from him." I kept calming them and silencing them until he finished his prayer. I then went with him to the lodging in the guard post, and he saw the change in my face, and he disapproved of it and asked me, and I informed him. He laughed and said: "And from where for me to be killed over a sunnah?" I said to him: "This is not permissible for you, for you are among a people who, if you stand up to it, will rise against you, and perhaps your blood will be shed." He said: "Leave this talk, and turn to something else."

God's words, "So I swear" (fa-la uqsimu): the meaning is "so I swear," and *la* is an extraneous particle (silah).

(By the twilight) (bi-l-shafaq), meaning the redness (al-humra) that appears at sunset until the time of the late night prayer ('isha' al-akhira). Ashhab, Abdullah ibn al-Hakam, Yahya ibn Yahya and others, whose number is large, related from Malik: "Al-shafaq is the redness that is in the west (al-maghrib). When the redness has gone, the time of maghrib has ended and the 'isha' prayer becomes obligatory."

Ibn Wahb related: "One who is not alone told me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Shaddad ibn Aws and Abu Hurayrah, that al-shafaq is the redness." Malik ibn Anas also held this view. Other than Ibn Wahb, among the Companions, the following are mentioned: 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Abu Qatadah, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah and Ibn al-Zubayr. Among the Successors (tabi'un): Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Musayyab, Tawus, 'Abdullah ibn Dinar and al-Zuhri. Among the jurists who held this view: al-Awza'i, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubaydah, Ahmad and Ishaq.

It was also said that it is the whiteness (al-bayad). This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah as well, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, al-Awza'i, and Abu Hanifah in one of the two reports from him. Asad ibn 'Amr related that he retracted it. It is also reported from Ibn 'Umar that it is the whiteness.

The preferred view is the first, because most of the Companions, the Successors and the jurists hold it, and because the evidence from Arabic usage, etymology (ishtiqaq) and the Sunnah supports it.

*"And one of a red hue, like the reddening of the shafaq."*

Another said:

*"Rise, boy, I mean one not confused by time, with a cup whose contents are shafaq."*

And the word shafaq is applied to red ochre (al-maghra).

In al-Sihah: "Al-shafaq is the remnant of the sunlight and its redness at the beginning of the night, until near the 'atamah (late night)." Al-Khalil said: "Al-shafaq is the redness from the sunset until the time of the late night prayer. When it has gone, it is said: 'The shafaq has set.'"

Then it was said: the root of the word is from the delicacy (riqqah) of a thing. It is said: "Shay' shafaq," meaning it has no firmness because of its delicacy. "Ashfaqa 'alayhi" means his heart became tender toward him. "Al-shafaqah" is the noun from al-ishfaq, which is tenderness of heart, and likewise al-shafaq. The poet said:

*"She loves my life, and I love her death out of tenderness, and death is the most honourable guest for the noble."*

So al-shafaq is the remnant of the sunlight and its redness, as if that delicacy is from the sunlight.

The philosophers claimed that the whiteness never sets at all. Al-Khalil said: "I climbed the minaret of Alexandria and gazed at the whiteness, and I saw it moving from horizon to horizon, and I did not see it set." Ibn Abi Uways said: "I saw it extend until the rising of dawn." Our scholars said: "Since its time is not fixed, its consideration falls away."

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: "I know better than you the time of the late night prayer. The Prophet ﷺ used to pray it when the moon had set on the third night." This is a fixed determination. Then the ruling is attached to the first (appearance of) the name. It cannot be said: "This is refuted against you by the first dawn." We say: the first dawn has no ruling attached to it, neither of prayer nor of abstention, because the Prophet ﷺ explained the dawn by his words and deeds. He said: "The dawn is not that you say like this," and he raised his hand upward, "but the dawn is that you say like this," and he spread it out. Its explanation has already passed in the verse of fasting in Surat al-Baqarah, so there is no point in repeating it.

Mujahid said: "Al-shafaq is the entire day. Do you not see that He says: *'And the night and what it drives together'*?" Ikrimah said: "It is what remains of the day."

Al-shafaq also means the poor quality of things. It is said: "A meagre gift (ata' mushaffaq)," meaning reduced. Al-Kumayt said:

*"A king, nobler than kings, whose hands pour out for those who ask, not sparing."*

God's words, "And the night and what it drives together" (wa-l-layli wa-ma wasaq): that is, it gathers, unites and wraps up. Its origin is from the sultan's force and anger. Had He not come out to the servants through the door of mercy, the servants could not have endured His coming. But He came out through the door of mercy, so He was gentle with them, and the creatures became calm in Him, then they were startled, gathered together and withdrew, and each returned to its shelter, and it settled there from its terror. This is His words, "And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein" (Qur'an 28:73), that is, by night, "and that you may seek of His bounty" (28:73), that is, by day, as previously mentioned. So the night gathers and unites what was spread out by day in its activity. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Muqatil and others. Dhabi' ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi said:

*"Indeed, I and you, with longing for you, am like one who grasps water whose fingers did not hold it."*

He means that there is nothing of that in his hand, just as there is nothing in the hand of one who grasps water. When the night covers the mountains, trees, seas and earth, and they are gathered under it, then it has "wasaqa" them. Al-wasq is joining one thing to another. You say: "Wasaqtuhu, asiquhu, wasqan." From this, a large gathered quantity of food is called "wasq," which is sixty sa'. "Ta'am musawwaq" means gathered together, and "ibil mustawsiqah" means gathered. The rajaz poet said:

*"Indeed, we have young she-camels, well-formed, gathered together, if only they found a driver."*

Ikrimah said: "'And what it wasaq' means what it drives to its resting place." So al-wasq has the meaning of driving away. From this, a herd of camels, sheep and donkeys that is driven is called "wasiqah." The poet said:

*"As a tracker follows the traces of the driven herd."*

(This is the words of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, whose first verse is: "I lied against you; you do not cease to track me.")

From Ibn 'Abbas: "And what it wasaq" means what it covers and conceals. Also from him: "And what it carries." Whatever you carry, you have wasaqtahu. The Arabs say: "I will not do it as long as my eye wasqat the water," meaning it carries it. *"He urged them on constantly, driving them until the tracks of the herd were distinct from the wisaq."*

There is also "mawasiq." "Awsaqtu al-ba'ir" means I loaded its burden on it. "Awsaqat al-nakhlah" means the palm tree's yield became abundant.

Yaman, al-Dahhak and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: "It carries from the darkness." Muqatil said: "Or it carries from the stars." Al-Qushayri said: "The meaning of 'carries' is that it gathers and joins. There is also "mawasiq." "Awsaqtu al-ba'ir" means I loaded its burden on it. "Awsaqat al-nakhlah" means the palm tree's yield became abundant.

That is, like one who acts.

Al-Sha'bi said: "You will surely ride, O Muhammad, heaven after heaven, and degree after degree, and rank after rank, in nearness to God Most High." Ibn Mas'ud said: "You will surely ride the heaven state after state, meaning its states which God described: splitting, folding up, sometimes being like molten metal and sometimes like oil." So the address is to the human being mentioned in His words: *"O man, you are labouring toward your Lord"* (84:6), which is a generic name, meaning people.

The rest read *la-tarkabunna* with a damma on the ba', as address to people. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this, and said: "Because the meaning is more fitting to people than to the Prophet ﷺ, given what was mentioned before this verse: *'As for him who is given his record in his right hand... and as for him who is given his record behind his back'* (84:7–10)." That is: you will surely ride state after state of the horrors of the Resurrection, or you will surely follow the practice of those before you in denying and fabricating against the prophets.

I say: all of this is intended, and hadiths have come with that. Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali, from Jabir, may God be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Indeed, the son of Adam is in heedlessness of what God Mighty and Majestic created him for. Indeed, God, there is no god but He, when He wills to create him, says to the angel: 'Write his provision, his traces, his term, and write whether he will be wretched or happy.' Then that angel ascends, and God sends another angel who guards him until he reaches maturity. Then God sends two angels who write his good deeds and his evil deeds. When death comes to him, those two angels ascend. Then the angel of death, peace be upon him, comes to him and takes his soul. When he is placed in his grave, the soul is returned to his body. Then the angel of death ascends. Then the two angels of the grave come to him and test him, then they ascend. When the Hour is established, the angel of good deeds and the angel of evil deeds descend upon him, and they bring forth a book tied to his neck, then they both attend him, one driving and the other as witness." Then God Mighty and Majestic says: *"You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp"* (Qur'an 50:22). The Messenger of God ﷺ said regarding *"You will surely ride stage after stage"*: "State after state." Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, before you is a great matter, so seek help in God the Mighty."

This hadith includes the states that befall the human being from the time he is created until the time he is resurrected, and all of them are hardship after hardship: life, then death, then resurrection, then recompense, and in each of these states there are hardships.

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "You will surely follow [in the narration of al-Bukhari: 'You will surely follow'] the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, so that if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it." They said: "O Messenger of God, the Jews and the Christians?" He said: "Who else?" Al-Bukhari recorded it.

As for the statements of the commentators: 'Ikrimah said: "State after state: weaned after suckling, and an old man after youth." The poet said:

*"Thus is the man: if a term is granted to him, after it he will ride stage after stage."*

And from Makhul: "Every twenty years you will find a matter you were not upon." Al-Hasan said: "A matter after a matter: ease after hardship, and hardship after ease; wealth after poverty, and poverty after wealth; health after sickness, and sickness after health." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "A station after a station: some people were humble in this world and are raised up in the Hereafter, and some people were exalted in this world and are brought low in the Hereafter." It has also been said: "A station from a station, and a tabaq (stratum, layer) from a tabaq." That is because whoever is upon righteousness is drawn by it to a righteousness above him, and whoever is upon corruption is drawn by it to a corruption above him, for everything moves toward its like. Ibn Zayd said: "You will surely pass from the stratum of this world to the stratum of the Hereafter."

Ibn Abbas said: "The hardships and terrors are: death, then resurrection, then the reckoning (al-'ard)." The Arabs say of one who has fallen into a severe matter: "He has fallen into the daughters of tabaq," and "one of the daughters of tabaq." From this it was said of a severe calamity: "Umm tabaq" (mother of tabaq), and "one of the daughters of tabaq." Its origin is from the snakes, since a snake is called "Umm tabaq" because it coils (tahwiha) around things.

In the language, tabaq means a state, as we have described. Al-Aqra' ibn Habis al-Tamimi said:

"I am a man who has milked the age to its last sips,
and a tabaq from it has driven me from one tabaq to another."

This is the clearest proof of the createdness of the world and of the existence of the Maker. The wise have said: "Whoever is in one state today and in another state tomorrow should know that his governance belongs to other than himself." It was said to Abu Bakr al-Warraq: "What is the proof that this world has a Maker?" He said: "The transformation of conditions, the weakness of strength, the frailty of the pillars, the subjugation of intention, and the abrogation of resolve."

It is also said: "A tabaq of people came to us, and a tabaq of locusts," meaning a group. And al-Abbas's words in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"He is transferred from loin to womb;
when one age passes, another tabaq appears."

That is, a generation of people. Tibaq al-ard means its filling (i.e., covering the earth). Tabaq also means a thin bone that separates two vertebrae. It is said: "A tabaq of the night has passed, and a tabaq of the day," meaning most of it. Tabaq is the singular of atbaq, so it is a homonym (mushtarak).

It is read as "latarkabunna" with a kasra on the ba', addressing the self (nafs), and as "layarkabanna" with a ya', meaning "the human being will surely ride." "'An tabaq" is in the position of an accusative as an attribute of "tabaqan," meaning a tabaq that exceeds another tabaq; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "latarkabunna," meaning you will surely ride tabaqs exceeding one another, or exceeding, or being exceeded, according to the reading.

From Ibn 'Abbas: "And what it wasaq" means what it covers and conceals. Also from him: "And what it carries." Whatever you carry, you have wasaqtahu. The Arabs say: "I will not do it as long as my eye wasqat the water," meaning it carries it. "The she-camel wasqat, yasiq, wasqan": she carried and her womb closed upon the water, so she is "naqah wasiq," and "nuq wisaq," like nã'im and niyam, and sahib and sihab. Bishr ibn Abi Khazim said:

*"He urged them on constantly, driving them until the tracks of the herd were distinct from the wisaq."*

There is also "mawasiq." "Awsaqtu al-ba'ir" means I loaded its burden on it. "Awsaqat al-nakhlah" means the palm tree's yield became abundant.

Yaman, al-Dahhak and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: "It carries from the darkness." Muqatil said: "Or it carries from the stars." Al-Qushayri said: "The meaning of 'carries' is that it gathers and joins. The night covers everything with its darkness, and when it covers them, it has wasaqa them." This oath is an oath by all created things, since the night includes them, as in His words: *"So I swear by what you see and what you do not see"* (Qur'an 69:38–39).

Ibn Jubayr said: "'And what it wasaq' means what is done in it, meaning the night prayer (tahajjud) and seeking forgiveness at dawn." The poet said:

*"And sometimes you see us righteous, and at other times he stands with us like one who is wasiq, the one who is girded."*

That is, like one who acts.

God's words, "And the moon when it becomes full" (wa-l-qamari idha-t-satqa): that is, completed, gathered and became whole. Al-Hasan said: "Ittasaqa: it became full and gathered." Ibn 'Abbas said: "It became even (istawa)." Qatadah said: "It became round." Al-Farra' said: "Its ittisaq is its becoming full and even on the nights of the full moon. It is an iftia'l from al-wasq, which is gathering. It is said: 'I wasaqtuhu, fa-ttasaqa,' as one says: 'I wasaltuhu, fa-ttasala.' It is also said: 'The affair of so-and-so is musttasiq,' meaning gathered upon righteousness and well-ordered. It is said: 'Ittasaqa al-shay',' when it followed in succession."

*"You will surely ride stage after stage"* (la-tarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq). Abu 'Amr, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, Masruq, Abu Wa'il, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, al-Sha'bi, Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *la-tarkabanna* with a fatha on the ba', addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: "You will surely ride, O Muhammad, state after state," as Ibn 'Abbas said. Al-Sha'bi said: "You will surely ride, O Muhammad, heaven after heaven, and degree after degree, and rank after rank, in nearness to God Most High." Ibn Mas'ud said: "You will surely ride the heaven state after state, meaning its states which God described: splitting, folding up, sometimes being like molten metal and sometimes like oil." From Ibrahim, from 'Abd al-A'la: "Tabaqan 'an tabaq," he said: "The heaven is turned state after state. It becomes red like oil (al-dihan), and it becomes like molten metal (al-muhl)." It was also said: "You will surely ride, O human being, state after state: from being a drop of sperm, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then living and dead, and rich and poor." So the address is to the human being mentioned in His words: *"O man, you are labouring toward your Lord"* (84:6), which is a generic name, meaning people.

The rest read *la-tarkabunna* with a damma on the ba', as address to people. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this, and said: "Because the meaning is more fitting to people than to the Prophet ﷺ, given what was mentioned before this verse: *'As for him who is given his record in his right hand... and as for him who is given his record behind his back'* (84:7–10)." That is: you will surely ride state after state of the horrors of the Resurrection, or you will surely follow the practice of those before you in denying and fabricating against the prophets.

I say: all of this is intended, and hadiths have come with that. Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn 'Ali, from Jabir, may God be pleased with him, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Indeed, the son of Adam is in heedlessness of what God Mighty and Majestic created him for. Indeed, God, there is no god but He, when He wills to create him, says to the angel: 'Write his provision, his traces, his term, and write whether he will be wretched or happy.' Then that angel ascends, and God sends another angel who guards him until he reaches maturity. Then God sends two angels who write his good deeds and his evil deeds. When death comes to him, those two angels ascend. Then the angel of death, peace be upon him, comes to him and takes his soul. When he is placed in his grave, the soul is returned to his body. Then the angel of death ascends. Then the two angels of the grave come to him and test him, then they ascend. When the Hour is established, the angel of good deeds and the angel of evil deeds descend upon him, and they bring forth a book tied to his neck, then they both attend him, one driving and the other as witness." Then God Mighty and Majestic says: *"You were certainly in heedlessness of this, so We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp"* (Qur'an 50:22). The Messenger of God ﷺ said regarding *"You will surely ride stage after stage"*: "State after state." Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, before you is a great matter, so seek help in God the Mighty."

This hadith includes the states that befall the human being from the time he is created until the time he is resurrected, and all of them are hardship after hardship: life, then death, then resurrection, then recompense, and in each of these states there are hardships.

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "You will surely follow [in the narration of al-Bukhari: 'You will surely follow'] the ways of those before you, span by span and cubit by cubit, so that if they entered the hole of a lizard, you would enter it." They said: "O Messenger of God, the Jews and the Christians?" He said: "Who else?" Al-Bukhari recorded it.

As for the statements of the commentators: 'Ikrimah said: "State after state: weaned after suckling, and an old man after youth." The poet said:

*"Thus is the man: if a term is granted to him, after it he will ride stage after stage."*

And from Makhul: "Every twenty years you will find a matter you were not upon." Al-Hasan said: "A matter after a matter: ease after hardship, and hardship after ease; wealth after poverty, and poverty after wealth; health after sickness, and sickness after health." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "A station after a station: some people were humble in this world and are raised up in the Hereafter, and some people were exalted in this world and are brought low in the Hereafter." It has also been said: "A station from a station, and a tabaq (stratum, layer) from a tabaq." That is because whoever is upon righteousness is drawn by it to a righteousness above him, and whoever is upon corruption is drawn by it to a corruption above him, for everything moves toward its like. Ibn Zayd said: "You will surely pass from the stratum of this world to the stratum of the Hereafter."

Ibn Abbas said: "The hardships and terrors are: death, then resurrection, then the reckoning (al-'ard)." The Arabs say of one who has fallen into a severe matter: "He has fallen into the daughters of tabaq," and "one of the daughters of tabaq." From this it was said of a severe calamity: "Umm tabaq" (mother of tabaq), and "one of the daughters of tabaq." "I am a man who has milked the age to its last sips,
and a tabaq from it has driven me from one tabaq to another."

This is the clearest proof of the createdness of the world and of the existence of the Maker. The wise have said: "Whoever is in one state today and in another state tomorrow should know that his governance belongs to other than himself." It was said to Abu Bakr al-Warraq: "What is the proof that this world has a Maker?" He said: "The transformation of conditions, the weakness of strength, the frailty of the pillars, the subjugation of intention, and the abrogation of resolve."

It is also said: "A tabaq of people came to us, and a tabaq of locusts," meaning a group. And al-Abbas's words in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ):

"He is transferred from loin to womb;
when one age passes, another tabaq appears."

That is, a generation of people. Tibaq al-ard means its filling (i.e., covering the earth). Tabaq also means a thin bone that separates two vertebrae. It is said: "A tabaq of the night has passed, and a tabaq of the day," meaning most of it. Tabaq is the singular of atbaq, so it is a homonym (mushtarak).

It is read as "latarkabunna" with a kasra on the ba', addressing the self (nafs), and as "layarkabanna" with a ya', meaning "the human being will surely ride." "'An tabaq" is in the position of an accusative as an attribute of "tabaqan," meaning a tabaq that exceeds another tabaq; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "latarkabunna," meaning you will surely ride tabaqs exceeding one another, or exceeding, or being exceeded, according to the reading.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ That is: what prevents them from believing after the signs have become clear to them and the proofs have been established? This is a rhetorical question of denunciation. It has also been said that it is an expression of wonder, meaning: be amazed at them for abandoning faith despite these signs.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾, that is, they do not pray. In the Sahih it is reported that Abu Hurayrah recited "Idhā al-samā' inshaqqat" and prostrated in it, and when he finished he informed them that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had prostrated in it. Malik said: it is not one of the obligatory prostrations ('azā'im al-sujud, the prostrations of recitation that are required), because the meaning is "they do not submit and do not obey in acting upon its obligations." Ibn al-Arabi said: "The correct view is that it is one of them, and this is the narration of the people of Madina from him, and the Qur'an and the Sunnah support it." Ibn al-Arabi said: "When I led the people in prayer, I left off reciting it, because if I prostrated they would denounce it, and if I left it out it would be a shortcoming on my part. So I avoided it, except when I pray alone." This is the realization of the promise of the Truthful (ﷺ) that the known will become unknown and the unknown will become known. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'A'isha: "Were it not for the recent nearness of your people to disbelief, I would have demolished the House and restored it upon the foundations of Ibrahim."

Our shaykh Abu Bakr al-Fihri used to raise his hands at the bowing (ruku') and when rising from it, and this is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i, and the Shi'a also do it. One day he came to me at the guard post of Ibn al-Shawwa' in al-Thaghr, the place where I taught, at the time of the Dhuhr prayer. He entered the mosque from that guard post and went forward to the row while I was sitting at the rear of it, on the openings of the sea, seeking the breeze because of the intense heat. In the same row with me was Abu Thimna, the captain and commander of the sea, with some of his companions, waiting for the prayer and looking out at the ships beneath the harbour. When the shaykh raised his hands in bowing and in rising from it, Abu Thimna and his companions said: "Do you not see this easterner, how he entered our mosque? Get up and kill him and throw him into the sea, so that no one sees you." My heart flew from between my ribs, and I said: "Glory be to Allah, this is al-Turtushi, the jurist of the age!" They said to me: "Why does he raise his hands?" I said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to do so, and this is the position of Malik, in the narration of the people of Madina from him." I kept calming them and silencing them until he finished his prayer. I then went with him to the lodging in the guard post, and he saw the change in my face, and he disapproved of it and asked me, and I informed him. He laughed and said: "And from where for me to be killed over a sunnah?" I said to him: "This is not permissible for you, for you are among a people who, if you stand up to it, will rise against you, and perhaps your blood will be shed." He said: "Leave this talk, and turn to something else."

God's words, "So I swear" (fa-la uqsimu): the meaning is "so I swear," and *la* is an extraneous particle (silah).

(By the twilight) (bi-l-shafaq), meaning the redness (al-humra) that appears at sunset until the time of the late night prayer ('isha' al-akhira). Ashhab, Abdullah ibn al-Hakam, Yahya ibn Yahya and others, whose number is large, related from Malik: "Al-shafaq is the redness that is in the west (al-maghrib). When the redness has gone, the time of maghrib has ended and the 'isha' prayer becomes obligatory."

Ibn Wahb related: "One who is not alone told me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Mu'adh ibn Jabal, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Shaddad ibn Aws and Abu Hurayrah, that al-shafaq is the redness." Malik ibn Anas also held this view. Other than Ibn Wahb, among the Companions, the following are mentioned: 'Umar, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Anas, Abu Qatadah, Jabir ibn 'Abdullah and Ibn al-Zubayr. Among the Successors (tabi'un): Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Musayyab, Tawus, 'Abdullah ibn Dinar and al-Zuhri. Among the jurists who held this view: al-Awza'i, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf, Abu Thawr, Abu 'Ubaydah, Ahmad and Ishaq.

It was also said that it is the whiteness (al-bayad). This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah as well, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, al-Awza'i, and Abu Hanifah in one of the two reports from him. Asad ibn 'Amr related that he retracted it. It is also reported from Ibn 'Umar that it is the whiteness.

The preferred view is the first, because most of the Companions, the Successors and the jurists hold it, and because the evidence from Arabic usage, etymology (ishtiqaq) and the Sunnah supports it.

Al-Farra' said: "I heard some Arabs say of a garment that was dyed: 'It is as if it were al-shafaq,' and it was red." This is evidence for redness. The poet said:

*"And one of a red hue, like the reddening of the shafaq."*

Another said:

*"Rise, boy, I mean one not confused by time, with a cup whose contents are shafaq."*

And the word shafaq is applied to red ochre (al-maghra).

In al-Sihah: "Al-shafaq is the remnant of the sunlight and its redness at the beginning of the night, until near the 'atamah (late night)." Al-Khalil said: "Al-shafaq is the redness from the sunset until the time of the late night prayer. When it has gone, it is said: 'The shafaq has set.'"

Then it was said: the root of the word is from the delicacy (riqqah) of a thing. It is said: "Shay' shafaq," meaning it has no firmness because of its delicacy. "Ashfaqa 'alayhi" means his heart became tender toward him. "Al-shafaqah" is the noun from al-ishfaq, which is tenderness of heart, and likewise al-shafaq. The poet said:

*"She loves my life, and I love her death out of tenderness, and death is the most honourable guest for the noble."*

So al-shafaq is the remnant of the sunlight and its redness, as if that delicacy is from the sunlight.

The philosophers claimed that the whiteness never sets at all. Al-Khalil said: "I climbed the minaret of Alexandria and gazed at the whiteness, and I saw it moving from horizon to horizon, and I did not see it set." Ibn Abi Uways said: "I saw it extend until the rising of dawn." Our scholars said: "Since its time is not fixed, its consideration falls away."

In Sunan Abi Dawud, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: "I know better than you the time of the late night prayer. The Prophet ﷺ used to pray it when the moon had set on the third night." This is a fixed determination. Then the ruling is attached to the first (appearance of) the name. It cannot be said: "This is refuted against you by the first dawn." We say: the first dawn has no ruling attached to it, neither of prayer nor of abstention, because the Prophet ﷺ explained the dawn by his words and deeds. He said: "The dawn is not that you say like this," and he raised his hand upward, "but the dawn is that you say like this," and he spread it out. Its explanation has already passed in the verse of fasting in Surat al-Baqarah, so there is no point in repeating it.

Mujahid said: "Al-shafaq is the entire day. Do you not see that He says: *'And the night and what it drives together'*?" Ikrimah said: "It is what remains of the day."

Al-shafaq also means the poor quality of things. It is said: "A meagre gift (ata' mushaffaq)," meaning reduced. Al-Kumayt said:

*"A king, nobler than kings, whose hands pour out for those who ask, not sparing."*

Had He not come out to the servants through the door of mercy, the servants could not have endured His coming. But He came out through the door of mercy, so He was gentle with them, and the creatures became calm in Him, then they were startled, gathered together and withdrew, and each returned to its shelter, and it settled there from its terror. This is His words, "And out of His mercy He made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein" (Qur'an 28:73), that is, by night, "and that you may seek of His bounty" (28:73), that is, by day, as previously mentioned. He means that there is nothing of that in his hand, just as there is nothing in the hand of one who grasps water. (This is the words of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, whose first verse is: "I lied against you; you do not cease to track me.")

"'An tabaq" is in the position of an accusative as an attribute of "tabaqan," meaning a tabaq that exceeds another tabaq; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "latarkabunna," meaning you will surely ride tabaqs exceeding one another, or exceeding, or being exceeded, according to the reading.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ That is: what prevents them from believing after the signs have become clear to them and the proofs have been established? This is a rhetorical question of denunciation. It has also been said that it is an expression of wonder, meaning: be amazed at them for abandoning faith despite these signs.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾, that is, they do not pray. In the Sahih it is reported that Abu Hurayrah recited "Idhā al-samā' inshaqqat" and prostrated in it, and when he finished he informed them that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had prostrated in it. Malik said: it is not one of the obligatory prostrations ('azā'im al-sujud, the prostrations of recitation that are required), because the meaning is "they do not submit and do not obey in acting upon its obligations." Ibn al-Arabi said: "The correct view is that it is one of them, and this is the narration of the people of Madina from him, and the Qur'an and the Sunnah support it." Ibn al-Arabi said: "When I led the people in prayer, I left off reciting it, because if I prostrated they would denounce it, and if I left it out it would be a shortcoming on my part. So I avoided it, except when I pray alone." This is the realization of the promise of the Truthful (ﷺ) that the known will become unknown and the unknown will become known. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'A'isha: "Were it not for the recent nearness of your people to disbelief, I would have demolished the House and restored it upon the foundations of Ibrahim."

Our shaykh Abu Bakr al-Fihri used to raise his hands at the bowing (ruku') and when rising from it, and this is the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i, and the Shi'a also do it. One day he came to me at the guard post of Ibn al-Shawwa' in al-Thaghr, the place where I taught, at the time of the Dhuhr prayer. He entered the mosque from that guard post and went forward to the row while I was sitting at the rear of it, on the openings of the sea, seeking the breeze because of the intense heat. In the same row with me was Abu Thimna, the captain and commander of the sea, with some of his companions, waiting for the prayer and looking out at the ships beneath the harbour. When the shaykh raised his hands in bowing and in rising from it, Abu Thimna and his companions said: "Do you not see this easterner, how he entered our mosque? Get up and kill him and throw him into the sea, so that no one sees you." My heart flew from between my ribs, and I said: "Glory be to Allah, this is al-Turtushi, the jurist of the age!" They said to me: "Why does he raise his hands?" I said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to do so, and this is the position of Malik, in the narration of the people of Madina from him." I kept calming them and silencing them until he finished his prayer. I then went with him to the lodging in the guard post, and he saw the change in my face, and he disapproved of it and asked me, and I informed him. He laughed and said: "And from where for me to be killed over a sunnah?" I said to him: "This is not permissible for you, for you are among a people who, if you stand up to it, will rise against you, and perhaps your blood will be shed." He said: "Leave this talk, and turn to something else."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 84, verses 22–25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nay, those who disbelieve deny﴾ Muhammad ﷺ and what he brought. Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning the family of Amr ibn Umayr, who were four, and two of them embraced Islam. It was also said: it refers to all disbelievers.

(And Allah knows best what they conceal) i.e., what they harbour within themselves of denial. This is what al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: they hide of their deeds. Ibn Zayd said: they gather of deeds, both righteous and evil, derived from the wi'a (receptacle) in which something is gathered. It is said: awaytu al-zad wa al-mata' (I stored the provisions and goods) when you place them in a receptacle. The poet said:

Goodness lasts longest, though time be long upon it,
and evil is the foulest thing I have stored of provisions.

And wa'ahu means he preserved it; you say: wa'aytu al-hadith a'iihi wa'yan (I retained the hadith), and "an attentive ear" (udhun wa'iyah). This has already been discussed [[See vol. 18, p. 263]].

(So give them tidings of a painful punishment) i.e., a painful, afflicting punishment in Hell for their denial. That is, treat it as if it were glad tidings.

(Except those who believe and do righteous deeds) This is an exceptive clause of disjunction (istithna' munqati'), as if he said: but those who affirm the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and do righteous deeds, i.e., perform the obligatory duties incumbent upon them, for them is a reward, i.e., a recompense not cut off, i.e., not diminished nor interrupted. It is said: manantu al-habl means I cut the rope. This has already been discussed [[See vol. 15, p. 341]]. Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn Abbas about His saying: ﴿for them is a reward not cut off﴾, and he said: "not interrupted." He said: "Do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes, the brother of Yashkur knew it when he said [[This verse was cited earlier with the wording: fatara hatfaha min al-rajʻ wal-ʻ... ]]:

Then you see behind them, from the swiftness of the wind, a trail of dust, as if it were scattered particles.

Al-Mubarrad said: al-manin means dust, because they cut it off behind them. Every weak thing is manin and mamnun. It was also said: "not cut off" means it is not bestowed upon them as a favour. Some scholars of knowledge mentioned that His saying: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ is not an exception, but has the meaning of "and" (waw), as if He said: "and those who believe." The discussion of this has passed in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 2, p. 169]], and praise be to Allah. The commentary on Surah al-Inshiqaq is complete.
